entry.title: fm-cli and Autonomix CLI get their own websites
entry.summary:
Two of the terminal tools now have proper homes on the web: fm-cli.ninepointlabs.com and autonomix-cli.ninepointlabs.com. Until today, the only way to learn about either one was its GitHub README. Each site is one page that answers the questions you’d have before installing: what the tool does, how to install it on your system, and how to get started. Both link straight to the latest release, and the full command reference stays in the README for when you need it. fm-cli is Fastmail from the terminal: a full-screen mail app, commands that print JSON, and a live watch that follows your mailbox over Fastmail’s push connection. The site walks through all of it, including offline mode, the two-week calendar agenda and contacts, and how sign-in keeps tokens in your system keyring. It also shows every way to install it: # On Omarchy omarchy-mise-install github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli fm-cli
# With mise anywhere else mise use -g github:ninepointlabs/fm-cli@latest
There are .pkg.tar.zst, .deb and .rpm packages and plain tarballs for Linux and macOS too. The README’s screenshot was also swapped for one showing sample mail. Autonomix CLI installs and updates apps straight from GitHub Releases. The site covers the package formats it understands, how it detects what’s already installed, the JSON output for scripts, and how it fits into Omarchy: the bar widget and the post-update hook that updates your apps whenever you run omarchy update. Install steps for Debian and Ubuntu, Fedora and Arch are right there, along with the full command list. A website is easier to share and easier to read than a repository. If you’ve been sending someone a GitHub link to explain what fm-cli or Autonomix CLI is, you can send them the site now. Nothing changes in the tools themselves, so there’s nothing to update. Originally posted on blog.ninepointlabs.com.

entry.title: Grounded Recovery Playbooks for Healthcare Appointment Assistant Retrieval Under Load
entry.summary: Short answer: make failure recovery produce a verified disposition, not a better-sounding guess. For a healthcare appointment assistant, keep source identity and revision time attached to every passage, retry only idempotent reads inside a fixed deadline, and switch to a clarifying question or handoff when evidence is empty, stale, or contradictory. I treat retrieval as an evidence pipeline with a stop condition. The language model is the last consumer of that pipeline, not its repair mechanism. entry.title: How a Clean Next.js Repo Ran Malware on Every npm run dev
entry.summary:
A codebase I got through Fiverr looked like an ordinary Next.js invoice app. It wasn't. Two dependencies deep, gated behind an npm auth token committed in the project's own .npmrc, sat a private package carrying roughly 180 KB of heavily obfuscated JavaScript — wired to execute every time the dev server starts. I caught it before running it. Here is the short version. package.json scripts held only dev, build, start and lint. No preinstall, no postinstall, no prepare. A grep for the usual suspects came back empty: grep -rnE "eval\(|new Function|child_process|execSync|spawn\(|atob\(|fromCharCode|base64" \ --include=*.js --include=*.mjs --include=*.cjs --include=*.ts --include=*.jsx --include=*.tsx . \ | grep -v node_modules
